sections.text: You chose the sharp Greco Attack with 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3. Black stumbled early with 7...d5??, and your 8.exd5! punished it immediately to seize the center. After both sides castled, you looked to build pressure with 11.Qb3?, though centralizing with 11.Re1 was more solid. Black retreated with 11...Nf6??, handing you a big initiative, but 12.Bg5 pinned the knight to the queen on d8 instead of the crushing 12.Ng5.

Black pushed pawns on the queenside, but you steadily redirected your pieces toward their king. With 15.Qc2 and 17.Ne5, you lined up against the g6 and h7 weaknesses. You pushed aggressively with 18.g4 to dislodge the knight on h5, but after 18...f6, you played 19.Bh6?? rather than simply capturing the piece with 19.gxh5.

Fortunately, Black missed the chance to hold and played 19...Re8??. You pounced with the decisive sacrifice 20.Bxg6!, creating a fork against e8 and h5 while dismantling Black's defenses. After 20...hxg6??, 21.Qxg6+! delivered a dual fork and exploited the pin along the rank, leaving Black no escape before 22.Qxg7#.

review.turning_point: The game was decided when you blew open the king's shelter with 20.Bxg6!, converting Black's passive 19...Re8 into an immediate mating attack.
review.focus: Look for simple material gains before complex attacks: on move 19.Bh6, taking the free piece with 19.gxh5 was cleaner and completely winning.

sections.text: This was the Italian with 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3, and Black went for the sharp 7...Nxe4. After 8.O-O Bxc3 9.bxc3 d5 your bishop was attacked, and you were a pawn down, though with a lead in development.

12.Bxc6?? took the knight but ignored the threat. You should have played 12.Qb3, which kept you in a playable game.
Instead 12...Nxd1 took your queen, and you resigned. It was a quick game, but the lesson is clear: after a check or an attack on your queen, look at the opponent's last move first.

review.focus: At 12.Bxc6 you took material without checking what 11...Nxc3 attacked. Make a habit of asking what the opponent's last move threatens before capturing.

sections.text: In this Italian, Black pushed too hard with 8...Nxe4??, and you took with 9.Nxe4!, the best move. After 9...O-O you stood at around +5, a full piece ahead.

Your 10.Bd2?? almost undid that, dropping the evaluation to +0.2; 10.Bg5 was the safer way to keep control. Black answered 10...Bg4, which put a pin on your knight on f3 against the queen. That was a good try, but you found 11.Bxb4!, the best move, and Black's 11...Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Nxb4 left you a piece up again.

You simplified smartly: 14.Bd3 Nxd3 15.Qxd3, then 17.Nf5 and 18.Ne7+ Kh8 19.Nxc8 Rxc8 won the exchange. Trading rooks with 22.Re8+ and 23.Rxe8+ then queens with 25.Qe5 Qxe5 26.Rxe5 kept Black with no counterplay.

review.focus: At 10.Bd2 you gave up the advantage in one move. In a better position, prefer the move that keeps tension, here 10.Bg5, over a casual developing move.

sections.text: You seized central control early after Black's imprecise opening. After 12.e5! you gained space, but 13.f4?? allowed 13...Nf2, dropping the exchange.
